entry.title: Jishou Akuyaku Reijou na Konyakusha no Kansatsu Kiroku.

results.review:
A female villainess otome anime story with a twist in it: the story is told from the POV of the male character of interest, which is not the one reincarnated, but the FMC is. The story is beautiful and will surely make you smile like crazy and laugh at times, especially with that twist, as the FMC is a free spirited person that does whatever she wants, first thing being confessing that she's the villainess to the MC directly, which is quite the bold move ngl. The MC is the perfect prince type that can do whatever he puts his mind to, actually mastering everything thathe tries instantly, but this also is quite a problem as he became uninterested in most things in the world, so following him throughout the story feels unique, especially because he needs to deal with the antics of the FMC trying to adhere to the scenario of the game.

While the POV of the MC is a strong plus in this story, I will also say that in my opinion it feels like a give and take for it, or at least in the anime, that is because we don't get to see that much of the FMC and her life in the story. This for me felt a bit like a problem, because I ended up wanting to see more of her and other characters that are gravitating near the FMC, but unfortunately, either because of anime time constraints or because they chose to, most of the things we get are from the MC's perspective and not from the FMC, which leads me to wanting to see more about the others as well, to be able to actually start caring about them better, and especially because they seemed interesting. From the comments on episodes though, especially towards the end, my understanding is that they cut out stuff that would bring more depth to the other characters, which is a shame, but they still adapted the main flow of the story, which is pretty nice overall. Might not have helped that at times, there were time skips, quite big ones at once, which might be from the original story, but it accentuated this feeling of missing parts.

The main story is a pretty standard story in terms of events and such, so while the story does feel unique because of the different POV we are getting it from, in the end it is a pretty generic villainess story imho. It is well done though, even if it is the same stuff done already quite a lot, so if you like these types of anime, it will surely bring you satisfaction watching this show.

Story: 8 -- Very interesting twist to have the story be told from the MC's view, but that also lead to the problem of feeling like parts of the story are missing, especially those that would build the other characters outside of the main cast

Characters: 8 -- Good characters overall, pretty standard for otome stories, but man, I wish I could see more of certain characters...

Overall: 8

entry.title: Toumei na Yoru ni Kakeru Kimi to, Me ni Mienai Koi wo Shita.

results.review:
I would consider myself a bit of a safe person in terms of anime taste; I tend to like what other people like, and I tend to dislike widely disregarded content. It’s extremely rare that I look at a score on this website and strongly disagree, except for comedies (which is so subjective that I hardly count it). This, this right here is the most dumbfounded I’ve ever been with a MAL score. Love Unseen Beneath the Clear Night Sky (or KakeKoi apparently) outscores Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia, the first season of You and I arePolar Opposites, Fate/Strange Fake, Goodbye Lara, and is close to the score of Witch Hat Atelier and Nippon Sangoku (I haven’t seen this one, but people seem to love it). I don’t like to focus on scores, I don’t think it’s productive, but I’m just trying to illustrate my expectations going into this as supposedly one of the greatest anime to come out this year.

This most certainly is not one of the greatest this year; not even close.

KakeKoi is really a tale of two halves. The first half is a romance between Koharu Fuyutsuki and Kakeru Sorano, with the “gimmick” of this romance being that our female lead happens to be blind. This worried me at first, as I initially feared Koharu’s blindness would simply be used as a means to empower the male protagonist. Luckily this is not the case. I am not a physically disabled person; however, the show seems to handle Koharu’s blindness with great care. There are themes sprinkled in about self-acceptance and a desire to be engaged with without her blindness being a centerpiece for attention. Unfortunately, outside of Koharu’s blindness the characters themselves are extremely uninteresting. While Kakekoi exceeds expectations with writing Koharu’s blindness, she doesn’t have anything else to offer as a character besides her blindness and her relationship with Kakeru. The viewer knows nothing about Koharu besides those two things. Kakeru’s even worse; the viewer is offered another light novel romance with a generic self-insert protagonist. Kakeru also has only two distinct traits: his relationship with Koharu and the fact that his parents are divorced. Unlike Koharu, his divorced parents serve zero purpose outside of justifying his antisocial behavior. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, there was just no real attention given to this fact outside of being told about it. It’s made worse that another light novel romance JUST came out last season that executed the divorced parents derived antisocial behavior better. 

I don’t think the first half is awful, mind you; there’s great ideas sprinkled in there. I’ve already talked about how Koharu’s blindness is handled, but dialogue in the show outside of the two leads is pretty decent. There are a few scenes in the show where several characters discuss where each of them grew up which I appreciated. The fact that this takes place in college sets this show apart from its contemporaries in general. The first half has its issues but it’s by no means bad, even if I was personally bored.

It turns out that the show got bored of itself and instead attempted to be Your Lie in April. The 7th episode hits the ground running with a shocking reveal regarding Koharu, and the story quickly spirals away from a romance and instead morphing into a tragic drama. The entire thing feels extremely forced; gone are the interesting themes discussing Koharu’s blindness, gone is the advantage of being in a college setting. The first half of the show tells you to engage with Koharu as a person and not endlessly pity her but then turns around and demands you pity her in this second half. It’s unbelievable how forced all of this feels. It’s not like this came out of nowhere, there’s some dialogue in the early episodes that suggested something was up with Koharu, but the two halves of this show could not work worse together. The show wants you to cry so badly but it doesn’t have the character writing to demand your sympathy, and it most certainly does not have the cinematography or soundtrack to compliment the scenes asking you to cry.

Even with how jarring and forced this all feels, I still had doubts within myself. Maybe I’m being overly critical to this second half because I was unengaged during the first half. Absolutely nothing could have possibly prepared me for the finale of this show. I take everything back, none of this was forced, this was all an elaborate setup for the corniest final 5 minutes I have seen in a long time. American Idol wishes it could set up a more blatant sob story. I can’t even tell you any more about how stupid this ending is without spoiling the show, but what I can tell you is that the suffering Olympics baton gets handed to KAKERU, because we need to cry for HIM too! This is ALL in the last 5 minutes of the show with no prior buildup and serves exclusively to remind our protagonist to never give up, because Koharu never gave up too. 

KakeKoi isn’t lazy with its writing, nor is it insincere. There’re genuinely interesting ideas that this show offers that set it apart. Unfortunately, more than anything, it is corny. It is a genuine attempt at a heartfelt story that spurs a suffering Olympics that make the closure of this series to be pitifully unserious and laughably corny. 

5/10 – Thank you for reading.

-🟢Spring 2026 Witch Hats, Wasted Potential xD A 13-episode anime that ends before anything interesting actually happens. It serves as an introduction to a creative world that nonetheless feels lifeless. This is arguably the least engaging first season of a potentially interesting series, as it ignores everything that makes the premise compelling.......... Plot: "Coco dreams of becoming a sorceress, although magic is only available to the initiated. When she discovers the secret of its operation, she unknowingly brings about a tragedy. Under the tutelage of the wizard Qifrey, she begins to learn magic, learning its possibilities, limitations, and dangers."--If I had to summarize this anime with a comparison, I would say it's "Harry Potter + Star Wars as medieval fantasy," but it pushes the most interesting elements aside and focuses mainly on simple and predictable didactic plots. After all, it's also an anime about school and the learning of magic by a group of little girls.

 We have two groups: the Pointy Hats (Jedi) and the Brimmed Hats (Sith). The former help ordinary people and keep the secrets of magic secret to prevent wars that broke out during the era of magic's prevalence. The latter are extremists who (it's not certain, as their storyline has only been touched on briefly this season) want to remove all restrictions on magic so that everyone can use it to fulfill their ambitions and dreams and push the boundaries of what's possible.
This seems interesting. The witch community wants magic to serve people, but in the name of the greater good, they impose restrictions on it (spells can only be placed on objects) that not only prevent the abuse of magic and wars but also deny access to magic that could heal and change the lives of many people for the better.
Healing magic is the only puzzling aspect of witchcraft law presented to us. On the one hand, influencing someone's mind is permitted for the greater good to maintain the system, but healing magic is absolutely forbidden, and aside from mentioning this, the anime doesn't elaborate on the issue.

 And that's exactly my complaint; all these interesting things were barely mentioned in these 13 episodes.
This anime leaves the most interesting storylines for later and instead stuffs us with child protagonists' storylines that reek of shounen-like pursuits of growth and becoming stronger, but with a more didactic emphasis.
The comparison to Star Wars is not without reason; a much more interesting plot direction would have been to balance the characters' temptations to turn to the dark side... that is, to use forbidden magic, yet this anime completely ignores this throughout these 13 episodes.

The most interesting developments regarding the main cast revolve around the white-haired teacher, who is divided into two equally authentic personalities:
- A kind-hearted teacher who has a very good attitude towards his students and their education.
- A ruthless maniac who will do anything to find the sinister witch organization.  However, these two personalities never clash. Qifrey is a good-natured teacher most of the time, but the things he does to find the brimmed hats never constitute a contradiction that would trigger any internal conflict within him. On the one hand, he cares about the girls, BUT he never considers that his search might lead to them being harmed.

Clearly, the most interesting character seems inconsistently written, which makes him more irritating than intriguing.
His character is also linked to the fact that despite facing dangerous extremists, no precautions are ever taken, and no one ever focuses on safety.
Qifrey and Coco, despite being aware of the threat, never even address it. Everything unfolds as if Coco had just arrived at the magic school and there was no threat. Despite numerous dangerous situations caused by the antagonists, nothing ever changes.
Worse still, the plot is often pushed forward by the sheer stupidity of the characters, especially Qifrey, who, after a significant incident with the antagonists, once again leaves Coco alone, not to mention previously leaving his students without any communication, despite the fact that he keeps a potentially problematic girl at his school at a high price for his own purposes... the credibility of the script is seriously damaged.

 The rest of the characters, for the most part, aren't bad (not you, Tetia). Almost all of them are different and have different approaches to magic and science, but their storylines seem uninteresting compared to the truly interesting things this anime could have explored. Perhaps they would have had a better chance if it weren't for the fact that the main cast is mostly children, so we get a lot of typical school storylines, including things like uncertainty about one's abilities even at the beginning and the need to understand that it takes time, the struggles of meeting family expectations, and the general theme of adults forcing children to follow a single path, ignoring their individuality.

These storylines are also hampered by excessive exposition, where characters explain everything thoroughly. "Show, don't tell" is a rarity here.
More than once, I've found myself scratching my head as a character explains something they already know in an internal monologue.

 The main thread running through the entire anime is Coco and Agott's relationship, which is written well for the most part, but only serves to develop Agott's character. The relationship from Coco's perspective seems truly shallow and bland, as her character seems unwavering, and the anime only gives the illusion that she has some significant internal conflict.
She will never give up and will keep trying until Agott understands that Coco is worthy of being a witch... that's it, nothing interesting. No matter how many times Agott rejects her, Coco will always try to establish a relationship with her.
It's simply bland, predictable, and boring, yet it constitutes a significant portion of the content of these 13 episodes.

Therefore, the biggest problem with this anime is its main character. Coco, as the main/most important character, is simply hopeless.
As I said, this anime only pretends that this character has any real internal conflict and well-developed motivations.  Her character is simply a good-natured girl obsessed with magic, which doesn't stray beyond the typical boring shounen protagonist who infects everyone with her optimism and inspires admiration for her pure intentions.
Any struggles she has are small things that disappear as quickly as they appear.
Her character doesn't pursue any real path or struggle with anything beyond trying to become better at magic.

How does this anime begin? With a serious tragedy that kicks off the entire plot—yet the show ignores all the consequences of that event.
For a protagonist who has endured such trauma, a natural storyline would involve grappling with guilt and the fear of the very thing that caused the tragedy.
Instead, these elements are merely touched upon briefly rather than developed into genuine plot threads.
Despite losing her mother, Coco never truly confronts her grief or attempts to come to terms with the situation; she is simply driven, never reflecting deeply on anything. The subplot regarding her mother is so insignificant that it feels as though the tragedy never happened—as if Coco had simply left home to study. Her mother’s story serves merely as a source of motivation, yet the narrative foundation for it is abysmal—from Coco’s internal experience to the lack of any established relationship between her and her mother.
This dramatic element is handled so carelessly that it fails to make any impact and feels completely forced.

Coco’s character is equally shallow, even when it comes to the magic itself.  Her love for magic is bland and shallow—a mere fascination sparked by the pretty lights she saw in childhood (the beauty of the magic lies mostly in the lovely animation; kudos to the studio). At no point does it evolve into anything more than "Oh, I’m a good girl, so I’ll use magic to help people." Even traumatic events involving forbidden magic fail to change this perspective or prompt any deeper questions; everything is resolved with the simple notion that "forbidden magic is bad, *but* the kind that isn't forbidden is cool"—and that’s it. Similarly, she never spends much time wondering what those wide-brimmed hats want from her, nor does she worry about the "morality police" threatening to strip away her memories... Why? Because she isn't a believable character; she’s just a puppet in the author's hands—a puppet placed at the center of events and given the most screen time in the anime... unfortunately.

World-building is the most interesting aspect here; however, rather than praising the creativity of the magic system, I’ll focus on the flaws—specifically, the world's sense of emptiness. After all, even the best magic system can't prevent a lifeless world from breaking your immersion.

Let’s start with the fact that the way the world is presented doesn't match the nature of the world itself.
There is no sense of the world's vastness conveyed through travel. Of course, not every fantasy story requires a journey—take *Harry Potter*, for instance: it features a massive, mysterious school and a few interesting locations nearby, which the characters explore without needing to go on a long trek.  WHA features a vast world, yet it doesn't feel that way; there are only a few interesting locations the characters teleport to, while the rest consists of the heroes' atelier and that single city they constantly visit.
A solution to this could have been a multitude of storylines—like in *Game of Thrones*—showing various regions of the world, rather than keeping us confined to one place with only occasional teleports to more interesting maps that nonetheless feel enclosed, causing the world to lose its sense of scale.

I also have a problem with the society in this anime.

Starting with the witch authorities, who guard the secret of magic, but we never see any action taken when it's common knowledge that someone outside the witch world has discovered the secret of Maggi. Okay, it's said that Qifey was given permission, but that also kills any credibility because in the witch world, where keeping the secret of Maggi is paramount, absolutely no one reacts to someone who "accidentally" discovers magic, and no one tries to investigate, no one asks questions, there are no factions, someone allows something, and everyone agrees?

The truly lazy worldbuilding makes the first half of this anime (the second half, actually, too, but I don't feel like writing about it) completely devoid of tension, even though the premise of a girl who could be a "threat to the system" requires that the system constantly put pressure on her... but as I said before, Coco's life is no different than if she had simply gone to a school with internet access to learn.

 The ban on magic for most people and the erasure of their memories upon learning its secrets is quite oppressive, and it's an interesting theoretical element of this world, but the viewer never really feels this, not least because of how Coco's case is treated, but also because, apart from Coco's, we don't hear about any other cases of people outside of witch society learning the secrets of magic.
People don't mention any other similar cases when they learn of Coco's existence, the moral police are never shown in any context other than the events of Coco. Nothing actually happens in this world, nothing is foreshadowed, no one (aside from a small, mysterious group of extremists who hide) is shown to be actually, even politically, acting on the issue of access to magic, no conflicts between witches and ordinary people... a void that makes the "magic is a secret" premise lose its real meaning, and the world seems to cease to exist beyond our characters.



 Someone who's read the manga might say, "Oh, but it gets interesting later." Okay, I'll rate it higher later, but these 13 episodes were completely unsatisfactory. The anime focused on generic, often poorly written storylines, and barely touched on the most interesting plotlines, leaving them "for later."

Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐❌❌❌❌❌❌

I really enjoyed Dandadan Season 2, especially with how the author spread out the romance between Okarun and Momo throughout the season. Instead of rushing their relationship, we just keep getting these small moments here and there that leave you wanting more. Their scenes together in the van were probably my favorite. I was honestly squeeing like a girl during those moments because they were just so sweet. At the same time, those scenes also made me a little sad because I found myself feeling jealous of how cute their romance is. There is something about the way their relationship develops that feels very natural andrewarding, especially because neither of them completely says what they feel yet. The season ending with Momo becoming extremely jealous after seeing the alien girl kiss Okarun was also a really fun cliffhanger. It immediately made me want to see what happens next, and I am already looking forward to the next season.

The action was also excellent this season, especially everything involving Evil Eye Jiji. I really like the way Evil Eye fights. There is something about his movements, expressions, and especially the sound effects that makes him look incredibly cool and badass whenever he takes over.

What I enjoyed even more was how difficult he was to deal with. Okarun, Momo, and everyone else had to resort to increasingly unconventional tactics just to contain him, and even after throwing basically every resource they had at the problem, they still could not completely defeat or get rid of him. I really like that kind of thing in action shows, where an enemy feels genuinely dangerous and the characters have to think creatively instead of simply becoming stronger and overpowering them.

Season 2 managed to balance the supernatural action, comedy, and romance really well for me. The fights were exciting, Evil Eye was a great threat, and the slow progression between Okarun and Momo kept me emotionally invested the entire time. By the end, I was already desperate for more.

I had a day off after working non-stop for a few days and just wanted to disconnect, so I binged this entire anime in one sitting. And honestly, as pure mindless entertainment, it works pretty well. That said, we’re not going to pretend the clichés aren’t extremely obvious. The first thing that bothered me from episode one was the whole “academic practical” premise. These are minors who are forced to fake a relationship with a randomly assigned classmate, even if they’re already in love with someone else and feel absolutely nothing for their assigned partner. Are you really going to force a relationship that one of them doesn’tfeel just to pass some school assignment? Imagine being in love with someone (like the protagonist is) and having to live as a couple with a person you don’t even like. Wouldn’t it make more sense to be able to explain the situation and, if you genuinely feel uncomfortable, switch to a different project?

There are episodes I genuinely enjoyed, like the fireworks one, but the series also leans pretty hard into fanservice. The girls all look like magazine models, every single one of them is unrealistically attractive, while most of the guys look completely average, just like Jirou.

Then there’s the romantic fantasy aspect. Yes, the show entertains me and lets me turn my brain off, which is exactly what I was looking for. But it also feels like a pretty unattainable fantasy for people who are single and end up projecting themselves into the story, imagining they could be the protagonist.

And here’s the funny part: I’m single too, but that doesn’t mean I can’t enjoy the series while still recognizing its limitations.

One more thing I want to highlight is the color palette. I really like it because it gives the show a distinct vibe. The colors are very strong and warm, making everything feel almost heavenly, like the characters live in some kind of romantic fantasy world completely detached from reality.

I think that aesthetic reinforces the feeling of watching something idealized, a fantasy where everything looks much prettier than it would in real life. Maybe that’s also why it’s so easy to get hooked, especially when you’re specifically looking for that kind of escapism.

In short, it entertains me, it has moments I enjoy, and it does a solid job of delivering what I was looking for.

Is it a particularly good show? Honestly, I find it mediocre. Is it entertaining? Definitely.

entry.title: Mushoku Tensei III: Isekai Ittara Honki Dasu

results.review:
One of the things I enjoyed most about this season was seeing how much Rudeus has progressed as a character. He is incredibly talented and powerful, but he is far from being invincible, and he still has plenty of flaws. I have always preferred main characters like this because they feel more believable. Despite everything he has accomplished, Rudeus is still capable of making stupid decisions and mistakes, just like any normal human being. Eris was another highlight for me. Seeing how much effort she put into becoming stronger, all because she wanted to be someone worthy of standing beside Rudeus, was genuinely touching. This madethe Oldeus Diary timeline even more painful, especially seeing how badly Rudeus treated her despite everything she had done for him. It really made me appreciate her character even more, and I am definitely looking forward to seeing more of her next season.

The high-stakes combat was also excellent. Despite Rudeus already being one of the strongest fighters in the series, the story never makes you feel like he can simply overpower every enemy he encounters. The world of Mushoku Tensei remains incredibly dangerous, and I love how the main characters often have to rely on teamwork just to stand a fighting chance against their opponents. Their victories feel earned rather than handed to them simply because they are the protagonists.

The tragedy was handled particularly well, too. I genuinely did not expect Paul's death. Normally, I am pretty quick to pick up on death flags, but this one completely caught me off guard. It was a painful reminder that even important characters are not necessarily safe in this world.

I do have one criticism, though. The introduction of time travel initially affected my enjoyment of the story because I generally dislike it when such mechanics are introduced into an established narrative. However, the more I thought about it, the more it made sense. Man-God never anticipated that Rudeus would become desperate enough, or that he was talented enough, to figure out how to travel through time. Looking at it from that perspective, it actually felt like a believable consequence of the characters' actions rather than a convenient plot device. What initially bothered me ended up being something I could appreciate.

As for the harem aspect, I honestly wasn't particularly bothered by it, unlike many other viewers. I've always had a soft spot for harem anime, but I can certainly recognize the difference between a harem that exists mainly for fan service and one that actually feels earned through meaningful character development. Mushoku Tensei definitely falls into the latter category for me, and I don't think it deserves the harsh criticism it receives simply for going down that route. Sylphie, Roxy, and Eris are all well-written characters with their own personalities, motivations, and development. Their relationships with Rudeus have been built up over time rather than existing simply to fulfill some fantasy. I can understand why Rudeus would find it difficult to choose just one of them, and frankly, if I were in his position, I probably would have made the same decision.

Overall, this was another excellent season that reminded me why I enjoy Mushoku Tensei so much. Its characters are flawed, its world is genuinely dangerous, and its emotional moments carry real weight. Most importantly, Rudeus continues to grow without losing the imperfections that make him such an interesting protagonist. I am especially looking forward to seeing more of Eris and how her relationship with Rudeus develops from here.

Monster is a series with a very effective narrative structure of suspense, especially in the way it develops Johan's presence through his absence. However, its psychological and philosophical ambitions, in my opinion, overshadow the depth with which it develops its characters. Tenma seems too idealized and morally unchallenged, while Johan functions better as a mystery and narrative device than as an individual whose psychology can be understood. The series raises interesting questions about identity, goodness, responsibility, and evil, but it doesn't always develop them through conflicts that transform its characters or reveal new dimensions of them. Furthermore, some subplots, the series' length, Kinderheim 511, andthe ending weaken my experience. Even so, I recognize its strengths in suspense, the narrative development of Johan, and several of its secondary characters. My problem isn't a lack of ideas, but rather the feeling that many of them remain unexplored to their fullest extent.

entry.title: Kamiina Botan, Yoeru Sugata wa Yuri no Hana

results.review:
My feelings about this anime are a bit torn. There are definitely cute girls, and they are doing cute things, but that theme seems at odds with them being a group of engineers in college that are into drinking, philosophy, and vinyls. Visually the show is fantastic and it is a pretty cozy cgdct. If you're looking for something cute to kill some time then this will be a good watch. The fixation on alcohol just makes it feel a little weird. I understand having a theme, and wanting it to feel unique, it just misses the mark for me. Along with the alcoholism theauthor ends up trying to do 3 things at once; showcasing alcohol, cute girls, and a bit of romance. It's too much hopping around without enough focus on one thing to really excel in a single 12 episode run. It simply wasn't satisfying.

I appreciate some of the more visual and implicit story telling. It's nice when authors trust the reader to understand without saying every single thing. The main part that bugs me is the alcoholic theme combined with romance, there is just so much consistent use of alcohol that it feels wrong. It's also a weak choice for a gourmet given that half of the drinks showcased are beers, that our main cast proceed to skull so they can get sloshed as fast as possible. 5 tallboys, and they're picking up more on the way back?? All to go dip your feet into the river on a date?? Why did you get an odd number of drinks for 2 people? I'm still annoyed about that. The other half are hard liquor on the rocks... I might not be the most interesting alcoholic in the world but even I think that's pretty weak when I think of gourmet shows like dungeon meshi or dagashi kashi showcasing their respective foodstuffs. No, reading a quote on a bottle of whiskey then saying it tastes woody doesn't count as gourmet.

Like always, when you have a group of girls living together they have to all be lesbians. I enjoyed the chemistry between each of the couples, each with their own relatively unique dynamic and a bit of meaningful character exposition. I get that all that is the standard trope, I just think it's a lot trying to go over everything for 3 potential pairings in such a short amount of time. From all of the pairings the main couple's fixation on alcohol is much higher, which ends up feeling melancholy. Even when they're having a good time sober Ibuki pulls a couple of beers out of her pocket so they can get drunk immediately. Cute girls needing to be buzzed during 90% of their screen time to do cute things is not peak.

entry.title: Re:Zero kara Hajimeru Isekai Seikatsu 4th Season

results.review:
I immensely enjoyed this season, especially during the failed loops involving amnesiac Subaru. The psychological horror, mysterious deaths, overwhelming enemies, and Subaru's gradual descent into madness were some of the most fascinating moments in the entire series for me. My enjoyment was easily at 9/10 during those episodes. I was particularly excited when amnesiac Subaru confidently declared his "counterattack" after suffering through so many horrific deaths. I genuinely thought he had figured out something extraordinary and was about to turn the seemingly impossible situation around through some clever, unconventional strategy. Unfortunately, my enjoyment declined after amnesiac Subaru merged with his original self. The story had spentso much time establishing how ridiculously overwhelming the enemies were, making the situation feel almost impossible to overcome. Yet after Subaru recovered his memories, everything suddenly started falling into place. Julius managed to overcome Reid, Ram could suddenly overwhelm Lye with the help of Cor Leonis, and the other threats became much more manageable. I understand that there are explanations for these developments, but the shift still felt rather contrived. It was almost as if everyone received a plot armor buff the moment Subaru regained his memories.

My biggest disappointment is that I expected a more unconventional resolution. I wanted amnesiac Subaru to figure out how to overcome these impossible odds through ingenuity, using everything he had learned from his repeated deaths. Instead, we got what felt like a fairly conventional series of heroic breakthroughs and victories. I don't mind the protagonists winning, but when the story establishes enemies as practically unstoppable, I want their eventual defeat to feel equally extraordinary without diminishing how threatening they were in the first place. The emotional developments were good, but they didn't completely make up for my disappointment with the narrative direction.

Shaula was definitely one of the highlights of this season. Her backstory, personality, and tragic circumstances made her one of the most memorable characters in the Watchtower arc. I was disappointed, though, that Subaru couldn't even show her a little more affection during their farewell. I understand his loyalty to Emilia, but considering Shaula had waited 400 years for her master and was seemingly about to die, would it really have hurt him to give her some comforting words or affection? He certainly cried enough over losing her afterward. At least the little scorpion gives some hope that she isn't completely gone.

As for Rem finally awakening, it was a nice cliffhanger, although it didn't particularly change my overall impression of the season. I can understand why that moment, along with the numerous emotional payoffs, would resonate strongly with many viewers.

Overall, the writing is still good, and I genuinely enjoyed the season. I just wish the author had maintained the extraordinary tension and unpredictability of the failed loops all the way through the resolution. The buildup had me expecting something far more ingenious than what we eventually got. It's still a solid 8/10 for me, and despite my criticisms, I'm definitely looking forward to the next season.

And I absolutely love that.

Well, by Season 3 I already knew what kind of monster Ayanokoji is, and somehow watching him quietly pull the strings still never gets boring. That is one of my favorite things about Classroom of the Elite. Ayanokoji does not need everyone to recognize him as the smartest person in the room. In fact, quite the opposite. He is perfectly happy allowing somebody else to receive the credit while he works behind the scenes. Season 3 gives us moreclass politics, alliances, betrayals and situations where students can actually lose their place at the school. The stakes increasingly feel real because intelligence alone is not enough. You need private points, information, allies and sometimes people who don't even realize they are helping you.
The developments surrounding Ryuen and Honami Ichinose were especially interesting to me. Ayanokoji repeatedly interferes in situations where, from the outside, you could almost mistake his actions for simple kindness. But knowing him, you are always wondering what future purpose he already sees that everybody else has missed.
That is exactly the kind of protagonist I enjoy.
And then we reach the final confrontation against Class A.
The chess match in particular was fantastic. It fits Ayanokoji perfectly: two intelligent people trying to read several moves ahead while the larger battle between their classes is happening around them. The fact that outside interference also becomes part of the situation only makes it more interesting.
I also have to mention the philosophical quotations again. Three seasons of opening episodes with thoughts from philosophers and intellectuals gave the series a surprisingly distinctive identity. I genuinely looked forward to seeing what quote would appear and how it would relate to the episode.
The supporting cast has also become much stronger by this point. Horikita, Kei, Ryuen, Ichinose and Sakayanagi are no longer simply pieces around the protagonist. They have their own ambitions and development, which makes Ayanokoji's interactions with them far more interesting.
Season 3 continues exactly what I love about this series: strategy, psychology, power games and one protagonist quietly standing in the middle of everything while pretending he isn't.
Ayanokoji rarely needs to raise his voice.
He simply moves the pieces.
Masterpiece once again.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.

Well, I honestly did not expect to love Classroom of the Elite this much. When this Anime originally came out in 2017, I had basically zero interest in it. The synopsis did not catch me, the trailer did not catch me, and for years I simply ignored it. Now after finally giving it a chance, I can say that was a mistake. Season 1 is a straight-up Masterpiece for me. The biggest reason is obviously Kiyotaka Ayanokoji. At first he seems quiet, detached, almost boring on purpose. But the more the season continues, the more you realize that there is MUCH more happening inside his head. He observeseverything, calculates people, predicts reactions and manipulates situations without needing everyone to know that he was responsible.
And THAT is what makes him so fascinating to me.
He is not the typical protagonist who screams about friendship and wins because he believes hard enough. Ayanokoji treats situations almost like a chessboard. People have strengths, weaknesses, motivations and uses. Watching him quietly move everything into the position he wants was probably the biggest reason why I kept pressing "next episode."
I also really loved the philosophical quotes at the beginning of the episodes. Quotes from Western philosophers and thinkers might seem like a small detail, but they set the mood perfectly. Quite often you only understand why that particular quote was chosen after watching the episode.
The special tests are another huge strength. On paper this is a school Anime, but it feels more like psychological warfare with grades attached to it. Alliances, betrayal, information, social pressure, manipulation — suddenly something as simple as a school exam becomes interesting.
And then comes the ending.
Without going deeply into spoilers: Ayanokoji's final inner monologue completely sealed the deal for me. It basically strips away any comfortable interpretation you might still have had of him and shows you how he REALLY views the people around him. That was the exact moment where I thought: yep, I need to continue this immediately.
The animation is solid, the atmosphere works, and the soundtrack supports the psychological tone very well. But for me this Anime lives and dies with its characters and strategy.
Season 1 introduced one of the most interesting protagonists I have seen in quite some time. Cold, calculating, manipulative and incredibly difficult to read.
I went into Classroom of the Elite expecting basically nothing.
I came out wanting Season 2 immediately.
WATCH IT.

I have made a severe and continuous lapse in my judgement. I do not expect to be forgiven. Calling MHA the anime equivalent of ‘Chips’ was wrong. And this season proved it. Season 2 of MHA elevated the already solid 1st season to NEW heights. With solid structure, incredible fights, and FANTASTIC WRITING. This season catapulted the show to the edge of my Top 10, after only TWO SEASONS.Plot:
This season consisted of 3 main arcs: The Tournament, the Hero Internships, and the Battles VS the Teachers.

Each arc was given the PERFECT amount of breathing room. Except for a few minor pacing issues, no scene overstayed its welcome.

The fact that we had 3 arcs in one season, with REALISTIC PACING, is crazy.

First, about the tournament arc. Yes, it’s a cliche. Yes, every Shonen anime needs one. But this tournament had some of the most insanely hype moments I’ve ever witnessed. Deku slamming his sled into a bunch of mines to go faster, the cavalry battles, Todoroki’s ICE MOUTAIN.

The music, the buildup... Everything. It was perfect. When Deku picked Tokoyami to be on his team, I ACTUALLY cheered. In real life. I jumped off my bed and started cheering out loud. My favorite character finally got the spotlight.

The tournament was DAMN-NEAR perfect. It delivered some of the best emotional payoff in Shonen, AND managed to show off the HUGE cast of characters. It didn’t leave anyone behind. In fact, the author (Kohei Horikoshi) introduced MORE characters to root for.

Despite the insane 20-character main cast, Horikoshi figured out ways to give us tons of info through quick characterizations. For example, exam grades. We get to see the ranking of results, from 1st to 20th. Every character is ranked, so you understand their academic levels within… What, a minute of animation?

Of course, there were still flaws. Some of the fights were based on plot armor instead of actual ability. The Bakugo VS Ochaco fight was stupid. How did she tank 50 of his punches? Taking even one of them should have blown her brains out.



Now, about the Internship/Hero Killer Arc. This arc was probably the weakest of the 3.

The plot was decent, and the author managed to give everyone a chance to shine. He also developed the world by showing us variety in the lives of Pro Heroes.

But there was one major issue: Pacing. The anime KEPT REPEATING SCENES. I probably saw the scene where Tenya declares he’ll destroy the Hero Killer 500 times.

Then, the Hero Killer fight took... 4 episodes? WAY too long for one fight. Meanwhile, we only really got 2 scenes of Deku training with his new mentor.

Despite the pacing issues, the actual plotting was FANTASTIC.

Thank GOD the Hero Killer didn’t get away. That would have been such an unsatisfying conclusion to the arc. But again, that’s why you KILL villains when they’re restrained. You don’t LEAVE them unguarded and just let them escape. Thankfully, the author didn’t go for the bullshit trick of letting the bad guy get away.

I need to praise MHA for its stellar foreshadowing. All of the ‘Random’ people that joined the fight were foreshadowed quite well. For instance, Todoroki’s Dad told him they were ‘Going somewhere’, and then he shows up to help Deku. That was actually solid writing, instead of the bullshit normal mangakas pull.



Finally, the Student VS Teacher Battles. Although this arc was only 5 episodes long, it’s probably some of the BEST Shonen anime has to offer.

First, the fights. They were structured and executed PERFECTLY. 10 fights in 5 episodes seems insane, but they PULLED IT OFF! (Guess we didn’t need 4 episodes for the Hero Killer fight after all, huh?)

The fights in this arc were some of the best Shonen fights I’ve seen. Reveals were foreshadowed, powers followed the rules, and solutions were REALISTIC. For example, Todoroki used the moment Eraser Head BLINKED to create an Ice wall. That’s STELLAR writing, because it actually follows the rules.

I have to mention how HARD the magic system is. I love hard magic. Plenty of anime try to get it right, but none manage quite as well as MHA. Every character has a unique ability governed by rules. For instance, Tokoyami’s dark shadow. He summons a shadow from his back that he can use to attack or defend. Naturally, it grows stronger in darkness, and weakens when in contact with light. That’s a tiny detail, but it’s SO MUCH BETTER than just giving him an omnipotent shadow that can do whatever the fuck he wants.

The attention to detail is staggering. When the Tail guy gets out of a chair, the animators DREW his tail sliding out of the chair. Another tiny detail, but it shows the thought put into the story.

These final battles had some INSANE foreshadowing. When Todoroki and Momo were fighting Eraser Head, Momo lost confidence. Todoroki reminded her that the 2nd vote she received to be class president (Back in Season 1) was HIS vote, because he trusts her.

WOW... Just, wow. The fact that Horikoshi managed to call back such a MINOR moment from Season 1, and turn it into character growth, is RIDICULOUS. This is some of the best writing I’ve seen, and BY FAR the best Shonen writing.

Also, can we TALK about the villains? They’re FASCINATING, and they feel dangerous. Stain was a fantastic villain. He caused damage, crippled heroes, and almost killed our main cast. MHA isn’t as soft as I expected.

In the final episodes of the show, we learn the backstory of Deku’s quirk and the origin of ‘All for One‘. Both reveals felt grounded, and they were given the gravity they deserved.

The plot gets a 9/10 from me.




Animation:
My Hero Academia is animated by Studio Bones, the studio behind Mob Psycho and Space Dandy.

This season essentially proved that they’re my favorite studio OF ALL TIME.

There were some sluggish moments. Of course. In the tournament arc we had too many stills and panning shots.

But other than that, the action was PERFECT. Movements were fluid and stunning. Todoroki’s ice, for instance, always felt like a force of nature. We witnessed it fleeting across the screen and halting everything in its path. And the ice MOUNTAIN he made during the tournament gave me literal chills.

I have to mention the Todoroki VS Deku fight. My fucking God. If that isn’t the BEST animation I’ve ever seen, I don’t know what is. The BLOCKS, man. The BLOCKS! It was essentially Sakuga PORN for a full 2 minutes, and it had me floored. I jumped up and actually shouted. I COULD NOT BELIEVE it was that good.

The animation was fluid in general. Punches, jumps, attacks. Everything felt real. It kept me IMMERSED in the story with plenty of Sakuga.

The animation gets a 9/10 from me.



Music:
You can probably guess what I’m going to say. Yuki Hayashi, you son of a....

Just when I thought it couldn’t get better, this man shocked me again. The score was SUBLIME. SUPERLATIVE. SUPREME.

Hayashi leaned into the unique musical identity of MHA and made the tracks MORE special. The Rock tracks had more drum solos, and the piano tracks isolated the instrument to make scenes more emotional.

The entire soundtrack shifted towards something more somber. Not only that, Hayashi created tracks that caused GENUINE fear. The Stain OSTs.

But Hayashi wasn’t limited to sad tracks. The track that kicked in when the old man asked Deku ‘WHO ARE YOU?’ literally gave me chills. CHILLS. JUST FROM MUSIC.

HAYASHI, YOU ARE A MASTER. 10/10 for this soundtrack.


Now, about the openings and endings.

The first opening, ‘Peace Sign‘ by Kenshi Yonezu, was an instant banger. Of COURSE the man behind ‘Iris Out‘ and ‘Bow and Arrow‘ was going to create a masterpiece. The visuals complemented it, showing us each character’s routines. I LOVED that little glimpse into their lives. A perfect warmup for each episode.

The second opening, ‘Sora ni Utaeba‘, is… A modern classic. I have no other way to put it. It was fucking unbelievable. The powerful, slightly raspy voice of the leader singer had me hooked after the first few seconds. And then you have the beautiful angelic chorus contrasting his harsh tone (SORA NIIII UTAEBA). Fucking brilliant!

The ending themes were fine. Solid music, but the visuals made them pop. I loved how we got unique characterization through the endings. We got to see the cast in a Fantasy world, which gave us more insight into their personalities.



Voice-Acting:
All of the VAs reprised their roles and enhanced them with even more bombastic performances.

Deku screamed his lungs out, Bakugo heightened his explosive nature, and Tokoyami farmed aura for the entirety of the Tournament arc.

The new characters, such as Mei Hatsumi, had surprisingly interesting voices. Mei had a distinct timbre that made me want to hear her out. Shinso also had a fantastic voice. Slightly raspy, but projecting gravitas.



Conclusion:
This Season of MHA is, without a doubt, the BEST season of Shonen anime ever created.

The structure was solid, the fights were GROUNDED, the animation was stellar, and the music almost made me bust.

MHA is proving to be way more nuanced than I ever gave it credit for. It managed to develop a wide range of characters, each with depth and their own motivations.

Take Tokoyami, for example. His Dark Shadow is uncontrolled emotion, and he works hard to regulate it. That’s why he’s so stoic in class.

I was planning on giving this season an 8, but after writing this review, I realize that’s insufficient. Every element was perfect, including the writing.

That’s why, finally, I bestow the honor of a 9/10 RATING on My Hero Academia Season 2. May all Shonen shows aspire to reach this level of perfection.

The season made me feel hype I haven’t felt since Mob Psycho Season 2. Thank you, Kohei Horikoshi.

The Good: - The art style is amazing and unique. There's nothing cookie cutter in this show visually and it keeps things interesting. - The character development is outstanding. They really do a great job of taking you inside the minds of the individual players and give quite a bit of depth to their backgrounds as people and why they play the game. - In a way it's a typical shounen power struggle type show, but they do it in a mature way that's not cartoonish or cringey like a lot of shounen can be. - Cool opening theme - I thought the ending was well done The Bad: - The artstyle is so unique that I found it somewhat exhausting at times as a viewer. It's hard to explain but I feel like it takes a little more effort to watch this show than it does other shows. Yes it pays off, but still it's an odd sensation.
- Sometimes it feels like the art is the star of the show over the story.
- As well developed as the story is it still seems like they rush through some of the background stories. That's more of a consequence of only having 11 episodes to fit everything into, but there was a lot of narrative they could have expanded on given more screen time.
- Though they do it well, it's still shounen power battle anime and there's an awful lot of mediocre internal monologue and other typical shounen storylines. The actual sports narrative isn't really anything fresh or new and things can feel predictable at times.

8/10, but honestly it's a 7.5/10 with an extra bump because of the cool art.
